top_level_objectives: Identify the major structural features of the DNA double helix, including antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and complementary base pairing.
Explain how DNA strand directionality creates 5' to 3' polarity and antiparallel orientation.
Describe the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase during DNA replication.
Differentiate leading-strand and lagging-strand synthesis and relate both to the semiconservative nature of DNA replication.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the overall three-dimensional shape of DNA and orient students to the double helix as the molecule being studied.
key_visuals: A large, slowly rotating DNA double helix centered in the workspace
Visible major and minor grooves along the helix
Color-coded strands emphasizing the two separate backbones
student_actions: Rotate and inspect the helix from multiple angles.
Identify the double-helical shape and describe what makes it a repeating structure.

scenes.brief_purpose: Help students recognize the building blocks of DNA and where they are positioned in the helix.
key_visuals: Sugar-phosphate backbones tracing the outer edges of each strand
Nitrogenous bases projecting inward toward the helix center
Base pairs visually linked across the two strands
student_actions: Select or inspect individual nucleotide components.
Match each base to its position in the helix and note that bases face inward.

scenes.scene_name: Complementary base pairing and strand direction
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how specific base-pairing rules and strand polarity work together to stabilize the double helix.
key_visuals: Adenine paired with thymine and guanine paired with cytosine
Visual indication of two hydrogen bonds for A–T and three for G–C
Labels showing one strand running 5' to 3' and the other 3' to 5'
student_actions: Compare the two types of base pairs.
Trace each strand’s direction to determine why the strands are antiparallel.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the start of DNA replication and the opening of the double helix at the replication fork.
key_visuals: A replication fork where the helix is being unwound
Helicase moving along the DNA and separating the strands
Single-strand binding proteins coating the exposed strands
student_actions: Observe the helix opening and identify the replication fork.
Predict why exposed strands need stabilization during replication.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explain how DNA polymerase builds new DNA using each parental strand as a template and why synthesis is directional.
key_visuals: DNA polymerase positioned on each template strand
Growing complementary strands extending in the 5' to 3' direction
One strand synthesized continuously and the other in short fragments
student_actions: Follow the direction of polymerase activity on each strand.
Distinguish the continuous leading strand from the discontinuous lagging strand.

scenes.brief_purpose: Conclude replication by showing how lagging-strand fragments are joined and how the final daughter molecules demonstrate semiconservative replication.
key_visuals: Okazaki fragments being sealed into a continuous lagging strand
Two finished daughter DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand
student_actions: Identify the role of ligase in completing replication.
Compare the daughter molecules to the original DNA and explain why replication is semiconservative.
